# Charli-Jo Tyrer

Canonical page: https://charli-jo.com/

I design digital services that everyone can use: directly, with assistive technology, or through an AI agent they choose.

## What I do

Most accessibility work starts with a finished website and looks for faults. I start earlier, with what people come to an organisation to achieve and what it can actually do for them. From there I model the service, build it with AI coding agents, and test whole journeys with screen readers and with agents, until people can complete them and can prove that they did.

I have worked in computing and assistive technology for about forty years. I trained as a systems analyst in SSADM and Jackson Structured Programming, spent around thirty years in the charity sector, including at RNIB, and ran my own business training blind people to use technology. I am blind, and I test with a screen reader because that is how I use the web.

## Three pieces of work

My practice rests on a principle, a method and a standard. Each can be adopted on its own.

### The principle: Universal Digital Involvement

A service should be designed from the outset to be open to all people, and to the agents they authorise to act for them. Nobody is an exception requiring special accommodation, whether they arrive by screen, screen reader, voice, braille or agent. Involvement is not something we do for people who might otherwise be left out. It is a property of a well-designed service, and everyone is in it.

[Read the Universal Digital Involvement proposal](/principle/)

### The method: Agent-First Accessible Service Design

The method revives systems analysis for the age of agents. It looks at an organisation from the outside, separates what a service does from how it happens to be built, models it around human intentions, and then builds and tests it. At its centre is the Completion Chain, six links that every journey must hold:

Intention, Understanding, Authorisation, Action, Evidence, Correction

[Read about Agent-First Accessible Service Design](/method/)

### The standard: Zero Information Casualty

Zero Information Casualty (ZIC) is a web design specification. It makes sure that whatever a site publishes reaches every reader, whether a person, assistive technology or an agent a person sent, without meaning being lost on the way. It asks four questions: can they read it, is the person's reader allowed in, did it actually arrive, and did it survive being read?

[Read the Zero Information Casualty specification](/standard/)

## How we could work together

Start with one journey. I look at your public website and services from the outside, with no logins, source code or hosting details needed, and reconstruct what your service actually does. Then I propose how one important journey could work for everyone, build a working prototype with agents, and test it. If it is useful, we go further. If it is not, you have lost very little.

- Outside-in service review
- A working prototype of one service journey
- Agent-first rebuilds of websites and services
- Zero Information Casualty audits
- Talks and training on AI agents and accessibility

## Get in touch

Email me at <hello@charli-jo.com>.

# Universal Digital Involvement

*A proposal by Charli-Jo Tyrer. Version 1.1, October 2026.*

Canonical page: https://charli-jo.com/principle/

## The principle

> *A service built for universal digital involvement is designed from the outset to be open to all people, and to the agents they authorise to act on their behalf. People may use it directly, through assistive technology, or by delegating tasks to an agent. None of these forms of participation is treated as an exception requiring special accommodation.*

Under this principle, getting people involved stops being a department, a programme or a concession. It becomes a property of the service itself, and it serves everyone with a stake in being understood: disabled people, every other user, and every organisation that wants agents to find it and act on what it offers.

## Why “involvement”

Digital inclusion is a recognised field, but the word has become passive. You are included by someone else, often after being labelled as needing it. Involvement is active: you are in the service, doing something, on your own terms or through an agent you chose. It also speaks to two audiences at once. A blind member of a charity and a business that wants AI agents to recommend it are asking for the same thing: to be fully involved in how services are found, understood and used.

In the UK, “involvement” also means user involvement and co-production, where people help design the services they use. That meaning is welcome here, and disabled people leading evaluation is part of the principle. But the main claim is wider: every person, and every authorised agent, can take part in a service on equal terms.

## The problem with inclusion as we practise it

For most of the digital era, inclusion has been remedial. We build digital services, then we worry about the people who can’t use them. We provide training, assistive technology, alternative formats, helplines and assisted-digital routes to bring those people in. However well-intentioned, this makes inclusion something added afterwards, aimed at groups labelled disadvantaged: disabled people, older people, people with little digital experience, people without the right device or connection.

That model asks the wrong question. It asks: who are we leaving out, and how can we help them in? It assumes the service is fixed and the people are the variable. It makes inclusion a cost centre, something to be funded, justified and, when money is short, cut.

Universal Digital Involvement asks a different question:

> *How do we design a service that is open to everyone, whether they approach it directly or through an agent?*

## Where this comes from

The idea that design should begin with everyone, rather than accommodate exceptions afterwards, is not new, and this proposal stands deliberately in that tradition. The social model of disability located exclusion in the design of the world rather than in people’s bodies. Universal design, developed by the architect Ron Mace and colleagues, argued that environments should be usable by all people without adaptation. Inclusive design in the UK, Design for All in Europe and Universal Design for Learning in education each carried the same conviction into their own fields.

Universal Digital Involvement takes that conviction and does two things with it.

**It applies it to digital services as whole systems, not just interfaces.** Accessible pages are necessary but not enough. A person can perceive and operate every page of a website and still be unable to find the right service, complete an application, or establish whether it succeeded. Involvement has to hold across the whole journey, from what someone wants to what they can prove happened.

**It recognises agents as a legitimate way to participate.** This is the new part. Increasingly, people will approach organisations through AI agents acting on their behalf. Some will do so because of disability, others because of time, language, confidence or plain preference. Delegating to an agent is not a workaround for people who can’t manage the “real” interface. It is participation. A service that turns away an authorised agent turns away the person who sent it.

## What the principle means

### All people

Not only disabled people, older people or those categorised as needing help, but everyone. Every route into the service, whether by screen, screen reader, voice, switch, braille display, phone, or an agent, is a first-class route, designed and tested as such.

This is a design commitment, not a promise that one interface can meet every need in every circumstance. No single route can. The commitment is that a service offers equitable routes to participation, tests actively for who is excluded, and provides effective alternatives where one route cannot serve someone, without treating those people as exceptions.

### And the agents they authorise

Agents are designed for, not tolerated. A service’s information, capabilities, rules and outcomes are available to an authorised agent in a form it can reliably understand and act on, with no need to impersonate a sighted person clicking through a screen.

### Within legitimate authority

Openness to agents does not mean unrestricted access for any software that turns up. Authentication, consent, privacy and security remain essential. What changes is the default: the ability to act through an authorised agent is designed in, with clear limits, rather than blocked by habit or bolted on reluctantly. Permissions are understandable, limited and withdrawable. An agent should never need to disclose someone’s disability or personal circumstances simply to discover what a service offers.

Organisations can have good reasons to restrict automated access. The test is whether a restriction is proportionate to a real purpose, and whether meaningful authorised participation remains possible. The key is to distinguish why a machine has arrived. Declining to have content used for model training, or refusing bulk scraping, is a legitimate choice. Turning away an agent acting for a particular person is a different act: it shuts that person out. A blanket block that cannot tell the two apart fails the test.

### With people in control

Involvement through an agent is only involvement if the person stays in charge. They must be able to understand what is being done in their name, decide what is permitted, verify what happened and correct it when it goes wrong. An agent that acts confidently and reports success it cannot evidence is not involvement. It is a new kind of exclusion with better manners.

## A guard against “everyone”

Designing for everyone has a known failure mode. It can quietly become designing for an imagined average person and calling the result universal. Specific barriers vanish into the general case, and the people who experience them stop being the ones who judge the outcome.

Universal Digital Involvement rules this out explicitly:

> *Designing for everyone does not mean designing for no one in particular. Disabled people remain the test of whether a service is genuinely open, and they lead its evaluation.*

WCAG and equivalent standards remain the baseline for interfaces. The principle sits above them, not instead of them.

## Five commitments

An organisation adopting Universal Digital Involvement commits to the following:

1.  **Involvement is designed in, not added on.** Every service is specified from the start for direct use, assistive technology and authorised agents.

2.  **Every route is first-class.** No form of participation is a fallback, and none is quietly unsupported. Where one route cannot serve someone, an effective alternative is provided.

3.  **Agents act within clear authority.** Permissions are limited, understandable and withdrawable, data is kept to the minimum needed, and any restriction on automated access is proportionate and leaves authorised participation possible.

4.  **Outcomes are evidenced.** People, and their agents, can establish what happened, not merely be told that it did.

5.  **Disabled people lead evaluation.** Services are judged open when disabled people can complete real tasks, directly and through delegation.

## How it fits with method and standards

A principle needs ways to be met. Universal Digital Involvement is the principle. Two pieces of my own work are ways of delivering it, a method and a standard, and others are welcome:

**Layer**

**What it does**

Principle

Universal Digital Involvement: services are open to all people and to the agents they authorise.

Method

Agent-First Accessible Service Design: analyses an organisation from outside, models its services around human intentions, and builds and tests them so that people can complete tasks directly or through agents, with evidence and control.

Information standard

ZIC (Zero Information Casualties): a specification that checks whatever a service publishes reaches every reader, human, assistive technology or agent, without loss on the way. It also distinguishes the purposes for which machines arrive, such as search, agents acting for people and model training, so an organisation can decline some purposes without turning away the people its services exist for.

Interfaces

WCAG and equivalent standards: the established baseline for accessible human interaction.

Each layer can be adopted on its own. A charity can commit to the principle without adopting any particular method or standard.

## For publishers and agent visibility

This is not only a disability principle. Organisations working on answer engine optimisation, generative engine optimisation and agent visibility want the same outcome from the commercial side: agents that can find a business, understand what it offers and act on it, whether booking, buying or enquiring. The architecture that lets a blind person’s agent complete a course application is the architecture that lets anyone’s agent complete a purchase. One build serves both.

Not every service wants to be found by every agent. A refuge, a safeguarding service or a confidential helpline may have sound reasons to limit discovery. Universal Digital Involvement applies to them just as fully: such services should still be usable by the people entitled to them, directly or through an authorised agent, even when they are deliberately hard for everyone else to find.

That changes the economics of accessibility. For decades it has been framed as a cost incurred for a minority. Agent involvement is framed as revenue available from everyone. When the same work delivers both, accessibility stops being the line finance cuts and becomes the work marketing asks for.

One condition applies. Universal Digital Involvement is about being understood truthfully, not about being chosen. Services should be honestly legible to agents: accurate about what they offer, clear about their rules, and able to evidence what happened. Techniques that game agents into recommending a service, or that hide its terms, work against the principle. Every step from intention to outcome counts, including evidence and correction, not only the steps that lead to a sale.

## What changes

If Universal Digital Involvement is taken seriously, several familiar things look different.

- **Involvement moves from budget line to architecture.** It is no longer a programme that can be cut, because it is part of how the service works.

- **Assisted digital becomes one route among many.** Human help remains vital, but it is no longer the only answer for people the main design left behind.

- **Blocking agents becomes an involvement question.** Turning away an authorised agent is assessed the same way as turning away a person.

- **Accessibility work moves upstream.** Instead of auditing finished systems, or simulating disabled users to find faults afterwards, disabled practitioners shape services before they are built.

## An invitation

This is a proposal, not a finished doctrine. I’m putting it forward because the arrival of agents is the moment to settle the question. Either agents become one more thing that digital inclusion has to catch up with, or we decide now that services are designed for everyone, however they choose to arrive.

I would welcome challenge, refinement and, above all, organisations willing to test it on real services with the people who use them.

> *Involvement is not something we do for people who might otherwise be left out. It is a property of a well-designed service, and everyone is in it.*


---

# Agent-First Accessible Service Design

*An introduction to the method by Charli-Jo Tyrer. Version 1.0, October 2026.*

Canonical page: https://charli-jo.com/method/

## What is Agent-First Accessible Service Design?

Agent-First Accessible Service Design is a method for understanding, designing and building services that people can use independently, either directly or through AI agents they choose to authorise. It combines established systems analysis with accessibility practice, AI-assisted development and the emerging possibilities of agent-mediated services.

The starting point is not a website, an application or a technology platform. It is the relationship between what people want to achieve and what an organisation is capable of doing for them. The method examines an organisation from the outside, reconstructs the services, information, processes and rules behind its existing interfaces, and develops a model of what those services should do. We then turn that model into a working implementation, which is tested against real human intentions and outcomes.

> *Understand the service before building the system.*

## Why a new approach is needed

For most of the web’s history, the page has been the organising unit of digital service design. Organisations arrange information into pages, build navigation menus around them and provide forms through which people request services or complete transactions. Accessibility work has largely followed the same structure, examining pages, controls and interactions to establish whether disabled people can perceive, understand and operate them.

That work remains essential, and WCAG provides a necessary baseline for accessible interfaces. But an accessible collection of pages is not necessarily an accessible service. Someone can navigate every page of a website with a screen reader and still be unable to work out which service meets their needs, how to apply, whether an application has succeeded or what to do when something goes wrong.

AI agents make this distinction pressing. Instead of navigating a website themselves, a person might simply say to an agent, “Help me find the technology training I need to get back into work.” The agent must then understand the intention, discover relevant services, establish eligibility, explain the options and perhaps help complete an application. The organisation’s services therefore have to be understandable beyond the particular pages, menus and forms through which they happen to be presented.

This does not make human interfaces redundant. It means the underlying service must be designed independently of them. Agent-first does not mean agent-only. It means designing a service whose meaning, capabilities, rules and evidence are available to people directly and, where they choose, to the agents acting on their behalf.

## Returning to systems analysis

The method deliberately revives disciplines I practised as a systems analyst, before the modern web and contemporary AI existed. Three ideas from that tradition do most of the work.

### SSADM: the logical and the physical

The Structured Systems Analysis and Design Method (SSADM) drew a central distinction between the physical system, meaning how something is currently implemented, and the logical system, meaning what it does independently of that implementation. It moved through four views:

**View**

**Question**

Current physical

What exists now?

Current logical

What does the existing system actually do?

Required logical

What should the system do?

Required physical

How should the new system be implemented?

These distinctions matter even more in the age of AI coding agents. A website’s navigation menu tells us how somebody once decided to organise information. It doesn’t necessarily describe the organisation, its services or the intentions of the people who use them. Rebuilding the existing pages with newer technology can simply reproduce the same conceptual limitations, only faster. Instead, the method reconstructs the organisation’s logical services from the evidence available, then designs a required logical system around human intentions and outcomes. Existing technology informs the investigation and constrains implementation where necessary, but it does not dictate the service model.

### Jackson Structured Programming: structure follows structure

Michael Jackson’s principle was that a program’s structure should mirror the structure of the data it processes. This method applies the same principle one level up: a service’s structure should mirror the structure of the intentions it serves. If people come with five distinct purposes, the service should be shaped around five purposes, not around whatever pages an organisation happened to publish.

### Entity life histories: knowing where things stand

SSADM modelled how each significant thing in a system changes over time. An application, a booking or an enquiry moves through states such as received, under review, needing more information, accepted or closed. Many failures in agent-mediated services are really missing life histories. Nothing tells the person or their agent what state something is in, so the agent reports success it cannot evidence. Making those states explicit and visible is the origin of the Evidence link in the Completion Chain.

## The intention and the outcome

The method distinguishes between what someone wants and what the service can demonstrably help them achieve. An intention might be: “I want to become more confident using technology.” That may need clarification. Does the person want to use a smartphone, learn workplace software, improve their accessibility skills or become more independent? The service should help them explore those possibilities without silently deciding what they ought to want.

An outcome might be: “The person has identified a suitable training course, understood its requirements and successfully enrolled.” An agent can complete a series of actions without fulfilling the original intention, and an organisation can deliver a service correctly without achieving everything the person hoped for. Designing around intentions and verifiable outcomes makes these gaps explicit. It also requires the service to describe its boundaries: what the organisation can provide, what lies outside its responsibilities, and when a person needs another source of help.

## The Completion Chain

At the centre of the method is a six-part model of accessible service completion:

**Intention → Understanding → Authorisation → Action → Evidence → Correction**

Every link is an accessibility requirement.

**Link**

**The question to test**

Intention

Can the person express what they want to achieve, including uncertainty or ambiguity?

Understanding

Can they discover and understand the available options, requirements and consequences?

Authorisation

Can they decide what should happen and, where appropriate, give an agent permission to act within clear limits?

Action

Can the task actually be completed, either directly or through authorised delegation?

Evidence

Can the person establish what happened, rather than relying on an unsupported assertion of success?

Correction

Can they change their mind, correct an error, withdraw permission, reverse an action where possible or find an appropriate remedy?

An individual page might satisfy WCAG while the wider service fails at one or more of these links. The Completion Chain therefore complements conventional accessibility testing rather than replacing it. It tests whether a service is accessible from the expression of an intention through to a demonstrable result.

## Agents on both sides of the service

The method considers two distinct uses of AI agents. The first is agent-assisted service construction, in which coding and analysis agents help investigate existing systems, reconstruct service models, build implementations, find accessibility barriers and make corrections. The second is agent-mediated service use, in which a person’s authorised agent helps them discover, understand and interact with services.

These are separate capabilities and must be evaluated separately. An agent’s ability to build an accessible website does not prove that another agent can use the resulting service effectively. Nor does successful agent-mediated interaction prove that the service works for a person using a screen reader without an agent. The method therefore requires three complementary forms of accessibility:

- **Direct human accessibility:** people can use the service independently, including with assistive technologies, with WCAG conformance as the baseline.

- **Agent-mediated accessibility:** authorised agents can discover relevant information, understand permitted actions and interact with the service reliably.

- **Human control:** people remain able to understand, direct, verify and correct what happens on their behalf.

None is a substitute for the others.

## Authority, evidence and trust

An agent-first service must distinguish between what an agent can technically do and what it is authorised to do. A person might authorise an agent to search for training opportunities, but not to disclose personal information or submit an application without confirmation. Permissions must be limited, understandable and withdrawable.

Services must also provide reliable evidence of actions and outcomes. An agent saying “Your application has been submitted” is not evidence that the receiving organisation has accepted it. The service needs to expose meaningful states, confirmations and, where appropriate, references that establish what has happened. Actions should also be classified by whether they can be cancelled, reversed, corrected or only remedied after the event.

Privacy and data minimisation are built into the logical design. An agent should not need to disclose someone’s disability, personal circumstances or membership details merely to discover what services are available. None of this can be left entirely to coding agents. It requires organisational decisions, human judgement and appropriate governance.

## How the method works

The method has six activities. They draw on the four SSADM views but allow continuous revision rather than a rigid sequence of approvals.

### 1. Observe the current physical system

Examine the publicly available service from the outside: its information, navigation, forms, transactions, contact routes, terminology and apparent organisational responsibilities. Access to administrative systems or source code is not needed at this stage.

### 2. Reconstruct the current logical system

Determine what the organisation actually offers, which processes exist, what information moves between them and which rules govern them. Record each finding as an established fact, a reasonable inference or a question only the organisation can answer.

### 3. Model intentions and outcomes

Identify what people come to the organisation to achieve: their intentions, possible interpretations, desired outcomes, constraints and the boundaries of the organisation’s responsibilities. Consider both people acting directly and people choosing to delegate particular activities.

### 4. Specify the required logical system

Design the services independently of any interface or platform. Model information, processes, permissions, life histories and states, evidence, privacy requirements and routes for correction. Apply the Completion Chain to each significant service journey.

### 5. Build with agents

Use AI development agents to create a working physical implementation from the logical model, with accessible human interfaces and appropriate machine-readable descriptions of service capabilities and permitted actions. Keep experimentation separate from production systems, with security, privacy, change control and human oversight.

### 6. Evaluate complete tasks

Test whether people can achieve defined outcomes, including assistive technology testing, agent-mediated interactions, verification of completed actions and recovery from errors. Failures feed back into the logical model as well as the implementation.

A working prototype may expose an incorrect assumption about a service, and testing may reveal that an intended outcome was poorly defined. The model is revised accordingly.

## From prototype to working service

AI agents make it possible to move from a logical model to a working prototype very quickly. That speed is valuable, but a convincing prototype is not a dependable service. The method distinguishes three levels of achievement:

**Level**

**What it means**

Model demonstrated

A working prototype shows how the proposed service could operate.

Service validated

Representative users have completed defined tasks, including direct assistive technology and agent-mediated journeys.

Production ready

Accessibility, security, privacy, governance, operations, maintenance and service continuity requirements have been addressed.

These levels stop the speed of AI-generated implementation from being mistaken for evidence of readiness. The ambition is to build quickly enough that ideas are tested against working systems, while keeping the discipline needed to deploy them responsibly.

## Migration without reproducing the old system

Reconstructing the existing website also produces a content inventory, a URL map and a record of uncertainties that need organisational confirmation. These support a separate migration process, much as SSADM treated data conversion as its own piece of work. Existing content must be accounted for, published links and bookmarks should keep working through redirects, and member information, live transactions, legal obligations and operational dependencies need careful treatment.

Migration constraints should be understood early, but they must not turn the new logical design into a reproduction of the existing website. The objective is continuity of service without continuity of unnecessary limitations.

## A practical first case: TAVIP

The Technology Association of Visually Impaired People (TAVIP) offers a suitable first opportunity to explore the method. The proposed starting point is an outside-in examination of TAVIP’s publicly available website and services. The aim is not merely to find accessibility defects or replace one set of pages with another. It is to reconstruct the underlying service model, identify what members and prospective members want to achieve, and demonstrate how those services could work through accessible direct interaction and authorised agents.

A small pilot covering one complete service journey could establish whether the approach delivers practical value. The wider questions of delegated authority and agent-mediated member services could also give useful material to an organisational AI working group. The project is currently a proposal rather than an agreed collaboration. Any implementation, use of organisational information or publication of a joint case study would require TAVIP’s agreement.

## What makes the method different?

None of the individual ingredients is entirely new. Systems analysis has long distinguished logical systems from physical implementations. Accessibility practice has long required inclusive interaction and meaningful user testing. Service design has long examined user needs, journeys and outcomes.

What has changed is the practical relationship between analysis, implementation and use. AI agents can now help reconstruct systems, implement designs and make revisions at a speed that changes the economics of development, while other agents increasingly act as intermediaries between people and organisations. The method brings these developments together while keeping human intention, understanding and control at the centre. It does not assume that an agent should always be used, or that technology can decide what a person ought to want. It asks what a service must make understandable, possible and verifiable for people to exercise meaningful choice.

## Questions for further work

Version 1.0 establishes the method. These questions are where it most needs testing and collaboration:

- How should a service describe its intentions and capabilities so that both people and agents can discover them, without creating another hidden layer that only developers understand?

- What is the minimum evidence an agent should obtain before telling someone that an action has succeeded?

- How can a small charity express delegated authority in plain language that its trustees can actually approve?

- Which parts of the method transfer to organisations that are not themselves accessibility specialists?

## The underlying principle

A coding agent can implement a misunderstanding in an afternoon. As implementation gets faster, the scarce skill is the ability to understand what should be built, why it should exist and what would count as evidence that it works. Agent-First Accessible Service Design puts that understanding before implementation. It treats accessibility not simply as a property of pages or controls, but as a property of the relationship between human intentions and achievable outcomes.

The purpose is not to make people adapt to systems, or to make agents indispensable. It is to design services that people can understand, direct and use on their own terms, with or without an agent.


---

# Zero Information Casualty

*A web design specification by C J Tyrer and Claude (Anthropic). Version 1.7, September 2026. Licensed CC BY-SA 4.0.*

Canonical page: https://charli-jo.com/standard/

**Version:** 1.7

**Authors:** C J Tyrer and Claude (Anthropic)

**Date:** September 2026 (v1.0: March 2026. v1.1: July 2026. v1.2: July 2026. v1.3: July 2026. v1.4: July 2026. v1.4.1: July 2026. v1.5: July 2026. v1.6: July 2026)

**Status:** Foundation Document

**Licence:** CC BY-SA 4.0

**Supersedes:** ZIC v1.6

## Changes in v1.7

Version 1.7 is written from an event, not a review. On 15 September 2026 the largest edge network on the web, fronting roughly a fifth of all domains, replaced its single “block AI bots” switch with three independent controls — Search, Agent, and Training — and began enforcing them by category at the edge. The taxonomy is this specification’s taxonomy: the sent agent, the indexer, and the training crawler, kept apart because time, agency, and consequence differ in each. §1.7 has said so since v1.3. It is now infrastructure.

The same event drew one of the three lines in the wrong place, revealed a class of reader §3.6 had no rule for, and added a fourth field to the Content Signals syntax this specification instructs implementers to verify. Each is addressed below. No requirement is loosened. Two requirements that earlier versions entailed are now stated, one check is added, and one clarification is made that no reasonable reading of v1.6 could have got wrong but that somebody else’s classification system now could. A site conformant to v1.6 remains conformant to v1.7 if its stack has not changed. Whether its stack has changed is the subject of this release. Section numbering is preserved; amended sections keep their numbers, and new material is appended. The changelogs of earlier versions live in those versions.

**The taxonomy confirmed (no change).** A specification that records its own mistakes in the document should record its confirmations there too, briefly. The three-class separation of §1.7, and the rule that no permission is bundled with another, are now enforced by a network that did not consult this document. This is noted and not dwelt on.

**The formalised Admission Casualty (amended, §2.2; new, Part Six).** The new defaults block the Agent class — explicitly including chat fetchers and browser-driving agents, which is to say the sent agent of §1.9 — on every page that carries advertising. The stated reasoning is that an advertisement signals a page a person was meant to land on and see. The person who sent the agent is landing there. She is simply not looking. §1.8 called this the Admission Casualty when it was a misconfiguration. It is now a recommended setting, page-scoped, on by design, and dressed as sound economics. §2.2 names it. Part Six tells a publisher behind that edge which switch to set.

**Mixed-use crawlers given a rule (amended, §1.7, §3.6, §4.4, §4.7).** The purposes of §1.7 are separate. The crawlers that carry them are not always: the conventional search crawlers of Google, Microsoft, and Apple index and train under one name. v1.6 assumed one bot per class and had no rule for a bot that is itself a bundle. §3.6 now has one. Where the operator provides a separate training control, the base crawler is treated as search and the training declaration is expressed through the control. Where no separation exists, the publisher must state which declaration governs the crawler, and the statement must be true. A declaration this specification could not previously test is now tested by §4.7 step 8.

**Reproduction to the sender is retrieval (new, §1.9; amended, §2.2).** The edge network’s new content-use vocabulary treats full reproduction as a use that forfeits trust. A sent agent reading a page in full, aloud, to the blind person who asked for it is full reproduction to the one reader for whom the page was published. It is retrieval, and it is the screen reader case in every respect that matters. §1.9 says so before a classifier decides otherwise.

**The fourth field, and a fourth purpose (amended, §3.6; new, §1.18).** Content Signals has gained an optional fourth field, use, and the operators the edge network designates as accountable must now offer an opt-out from AI-generated search summaries. The field is permitted and not required. The summary opt-out is a fourth purpose, neither indexing nor training, and this specification declares nothing it cannot declare machine-readably in a standard field. §1.18 states the position and the condition under which it will change.

**The edge that declares for you (amended, §3.6; Part Six).** The edge network’s managed robots.txt, and the preference-sync feature replacing it, write a Content-Signal line that states search and ai-train and is silent on ai-input, inside a wildcard user-agent block. Silence on ai-input has been non-compliant since v1.3. A publisher who lets the edge write the file has a file that fails §3.3, and may have two blocks that disagree. This is stated, and the fix is one line.

**Declaration is not compliance, third fact (amended, §3.6).** v1.4 gave two reasons a robots.txt can be sincere and false. A third is added: the edge now enforces by category, “verified” no longer means “allowed”, and under the mixed-use rule a site that declared search=yes in July and blocked training at the edge began refusing Googlebot on 15 September without a byte of its own files changing. A declaration is true of a stack at a moment. Part Seven item 6 now says so.

**The crawler list redated (amended, §3.6).** The list carried “as of July 2026” and asked to be reviewed twice a year. This is the review. \# Preamble

This document specifies the Zero Information Casualty (ZIC) design standard for websites and web-based documents. It defines a philosophy, a set of design principles, and a technical specification. It is intended to function simultaneously as a publishable manifesto, a theme readme, and a briefing document for AI models working on ZIC-compliant projects.

ZIC was developed by C J Tyrer in the context of the CharliVerse intellectual ecosystem, grounded in the Tyrer Framework for accessibility and the Inference Space model of human-AI interaction. The name derives directly from the Information Casualty concept: an event in which relevant information fails to reach an observer in time to inform perception, action, or participation. ZIC sites are designed so that no such event can occur.

Version 1.0 ensured that no visitor who arrives loses any meaning. Version 1.1 extended the standard from guarantee to invitation. Version 1.2 addressed the case both earlier versions assumed away: whether the document arrived at all. Version 1.3 separated immediate human access from later machine use, and required service to the sent agent with honest, independent declarations about search indexing and model training.

Version 1.4 separates the standard from the appearance of the site that first implemented it. Every version to date has been written alongside charli.info, and charli.info is austere. Austerity was a choice its publisher made and was never a requirement this specification had any business imposing. A standard that tells a publisher to abandon her typeface has stopped describing access and started describing taste, and it will be refused by exactly the people it most needs to persuade.

Version 1.4.1 stated the specification's jurisdiction. Version 1.5 recovered the founding definition in full — information must reach an observer in time to inform perception, action, or participation — and found inside it the derivations of the skip link and the focus ring, together with a second governing principle that had been doing unnamed work since v1.0. Version 1.6 names the seam between what the framework derives and what measurement supplies, defines the words the specification binds with, and bounds every check by what it can honestly prove. Version 1.7 records the moment the three-class separation of §1.7 became infrastructure, and answers the three things that infrastructure got wrong or left unsaid: it names the edge default that blocks the sent agent from pages carrying advertising as the Admission Casualty it is; it gives a rule for the crawler that indexes and trains under one name; and it states that a page read in full to the person who asked for it has been retrieved, not reproduced.

The rule underneath was always simpler than the list of prohibitions that grew on top of it. It is stated in §1.11, and it fits in one sentence. As of this version it has a companion of equal rank, stated in §1.16, and that fits in one sentence too.

## Part One: The Philosophy

### 1.1 The Central Claim

A Zero Information Casualty site is one in which no person — whether reading directly, using assistive technology, or acting through an agent they sent — loses access to public meaning due to how the site is rendered, admitted, or delivered.

The sent-agent case is decisive. When a person asks a machine reader to obtain public information, the machine reader is their means of access. Refusing it is refusing them.

This is not an accessibility compliance target. It is a design constraint that shapes every decision about how meaning is encoded, admitted, and served.

### 1.2 Who the Site Is Designed For

ZIC sites are designed for the semantic layer first.

Agents, screen readers, search indexers, and voice interfaces all operate on the semantic layer of a document. They read structure, hierarchy, metadata, and text. They do not read drop shadows, colour palettes, or custom fonts — and, critically, they do not need to, because nothing that matters is kept there.

The visual layer is a rendering. For a sighted visitor, the browser produces a visual rendering of the semantic layer. That rendering may be as considered, branded, beautiful, or plain as its publisher wishes. What it may not be is the only place a piece of information exists.

An agent reading a ZIC site should receive the same quality and completeness of information as a sighted human reading the same page. If those two experiences diverge in information, the site is not ZIC-compliant. If they diverge in appearance, that is what appearance is for.

### 1.3 The Convergence Principle

Agents and screen readers are functionally equivalent at the structural level. Both:

- Navigate by semantic landmarks, headings, and links

- Require that link text describes its destination

- Require that heading hierarchy reflects content hierarchy

- Require that reading order in the DOM matches intended reading order

- Cannot interpret meaning carried only by visual properties such as colour or position

This convergence is not incidental. Information encoded in the visual layer alone is information that has been made inaccessible to a significant and growing portion of all information consumers. As AI agents become primary information consumers alongside humans, the case for visual-only encoding collapses entirely.

The equivalence is real, and it is local. It holds inside the document. It does not hold outside it, and §1.13 states where it stops.

### 1.4 The Tyrer Framework Connection

ZIC is the practical implementation of principles derived from the Tyrer Framework, specifically:

**Tyrer's Law:** In open technological systems, inaccessibility tends to increase over time as interfaces drift toward the dominant sensory modality of their designers.

ZIC is a structural defence against this drift. By requiring that meaning live in the semantic layer, rather than accumulating in the visual one, ZIC sites resist the natural tendency of a system to encode more and more of itself in the sense its designers happen to have.

**Classical versus Generative Accessibility:** Classical accessibility retrofits access onto fixed visual artefacts. ZIC is an expression of Generative Accessibility — information rendered natively from shared semantic source data into whatever form the visitor's context requires.

### 1.5 Why ZIC Sites Age Differently

Visual design trends date. Semantic structure does not.

A ZIC site built in 2026 will be as readable by whatever agents exist in 2036 as it is today, because its meaning was never held in visual conventions that drift. Its appearance may date. Its information will not.

### 1.6 The Open Door

Version 1.0 guaranteed that no meaning is lost by a visitor who arrives. Version 1.1 added invitation. Version 1.3 stated exactly who must be invited: every machine reader acting on behalf of a person seeking public information.

The web increasingly places bot-detection walls, JavaScript gauntlets, crawler blocks, rate limits, and policy layers between information and the people who ask agents to obtain it. To the person waiting for an answer, the technical category of the obstruction is irrelevant. Their chosen reader reached the door and was turned away.

A ZIC site therefore keeps an Open Door for sent agents. This does not require a publisher to permit search indexing or model training, and it does not bypass authentication, payment, privacy, or other conditions applied equally to human visitors. It requires that public content available to a person is also available, without agent-specific obstruction, to the machine reader that person sent.

The Open Door has three components, specified technically in Part Three:

**Service.** The site explicitly allows known user-directed retrieval agents and does not challenge, degrade, delay, or cloak their access to public content.

**Orientation.** The site publishes a curated map in the form agents natively read: Markdown at /llms.txt. Where practical, the content itself is also available as generated Markdown mirrors.

**Policy clarity.** The site states its content licence and independently declares whether search indexing and model training are permitted. Permission for one purpose is never inferred from another.

A note on honesty, in keeping with the rest of this document: as of mid-2026, most AI crawlers do not yet fetch /llms.txt, and its measurable effect on AI search visibility is approximately zero. The file's demonstrated use is in the agentic layer — coding agents, research agents, and user-directed fetchers that consume it as a routing map — and in tooling such as Lighthouse's Agentic Browsing audits. ZIC requires it anyway, for the same reason ZIC requires correct heading hierarchy on a page no screen reader has yet visited: the standard specifies what a well-formed site is, not what current crawlers happen to reward. The cost is one Markdown file. The claim it makes is the whole thesis of this specification.

That sentence is load-bearing, and in v1.3 it was contradicted three sections later. See §3.3.

### 1.7 The Immediate Duty and the Two Later Permissions

Machine readers arrive for three materially different purposes. ZIC treats them separately because time, agency, and consequence are different in each case.

**Sent agents: serve now.** A person has made a present request and is waiting for the result. The agent may be retrieving, reading, summarising, comparing, navigating, transforming, or acting on public information for that person. ZIC conformance requires that this class is admitted. Machine-readable declaration: ai-input=yes.

**Search indexers: discover later.** An index is being prepared so that an unknown future person may find the information. No present human request is being carried. The publisher may permit or decline indexing. Machine-readable declaration: search=yes or search=no.

**Training crawlers: model later.** Content is being gathered to shape a future model. No present human request is being carried. The publisher may permit or decline training. Machine-readable declaration: ai-train=yes or ai-train=no.

The structure is one duty followed by two independent permissions: serve the person's agent now; declare separately whether the material may be indexed later and whether it may be used for training later.

**No bundled permission.** Permission for a sent agent to retrieve public information implies permission for neither search indexing nor model training. Permission for search indexing does not imply permission for model training. Permission for model training does not imply permission for search indexing. Each purpose must be declared and interpreted independently.

**No profiles or levels.** ZIC defines one binary conformance bar. Search and training declarations describe publisher policy; they are not grades, profiles, postures, medals, or stars. A site is conformant or it is not.

**Mixed-use crawlers (new in v1.7).** The three purposes are separate. The readers that carry them are not always. A crawler that indexes and trains under a single name is a bundle, and a publisher who declares search=yes and ai-train=no has said two things that one crawler may be unable to hear separately. This specification does not resolve the conflict by choosing for the publisher. It requires that the conflict be resolved, that the resolution be declared, and that the declaration be true of what the crawler actually receives. The rule is in §3.6; the check is in §4.7.

### 1.8 The Casualties (amended in v1.5)

An Information Casualty is an event in which relevant information fails to **reach** an observer **in time** to inform perception, action, or participation. That is the founding definition, and every word of it works. *Reach* means the failure may occur anywhere between the publisher and the reader — in the encoding, at the door, on the wire, or inside the machine that read it. *In time* means that arrival at prohibitive cost or intolerable delay is a failure of arrival. A reader forced to labour for information that another reader receives at a glance has not been served equally; she has been served late. The four classes below are the four places the failure can occur. The definition is one.

Everything in v1.0 assumed the document arrived. Everything in v1.3 assumed that once the document arrived and was admitted, it was understood. Both assumptions are false often enough to matter.

We therefore name four classes.

**The Rendering Casualty.** The document arrived and was admitted, but its meaning was encoded in a way the observer could not decode. Colour as information. An unlabelled image that carries content. A heading that is only large. This is the concern of ZIC v1.0, and its governing principle is stated in §1.11.

**The Admission Casualty.** The document existed and could have been decoded, but a person was denied it because the machine reader they sent was refused, challenged, degraded, delayed, or misled. This is the concern of ZIC v1.1, narrowed precisely in v1.3.

**The Delivery Casualty.** The document existed, the observer was welcome, and it never arrived. This is the concern of ZIC v1.2.

**The Reconstruction Casualty (new in v1.4).** The document arrived, the reader was admitted, the meaning was decodable — and the machine reader reconstructed it wrong, silently, and reported the result to the person with confidence.

The four questions, in order:

- Can they read it? (v1.0)

- Is the person's reader allowed in? (v1.1, clarified in v1.3)

- Did it actually arrive? (v1.2)

- Did it survive being read? (v1.4)

**Why the Delivery Casualty deserves separate naming.** It is invisible to every check that runs against a document you already hold. WAVE, axe, Lighthouse, the HTML validator, the Schema validator, and a screen reader test will all pass a page that no visitor on earth can fetch, because every one of those tools begins by loading the page successfully. A tool that has the document cannot tell you the document is unreachable. The failure is upstream of the entire toolchain.

This is not hypothetical. The first ZIC implementation, charli.info, spent several days in exactly this state: immaculate semantic HTML, AAA contrast, and a robots.txt explicitly welcoming named agents — served over HTTPS behind a TLS certificate issued for \*.github.io, a domain it does not own. The certificate was valid. The certificate was trusted. The certificate was for somebody else. Every automated agent validating the hostname failed the handshake, could not retrieve robots.txt, failed closed, and reported the site as disallowing automated access. The site was, in the plainest terms, perfect and unreachable.

The defect was found by exactly one check: a human asked a live AI assistant to fetch the site and it could not. That check exists in v1.1 as §4.4, where it reads as the oddest item on the list. It is now understood to be the most important one, and Part Four §4.7 generalises it.

The core delivery test: does the document arrive at a plain client that does not already trust you? If you cannot answer that from outside your own machine, you do not know whether your site works.

**Why the Reconstruction Casualty deserves separate naming.** It is the one casualty with no analogue in screen reader testing, and therefore the one that the convergence principle cannot reach.

A blind human reading a badly structured page knows that something is wrong. She backtracks. She re-reads. She hunts for the heading that should have been there. Her confusion is information, and it is available to her in the moment.

A machine reader does not backtrack. Faced with ambiguity — an unlabelled table, an implied hierarchy, a list that is only a list visually, a figure whose caption is three elements away — it resolves the ambiguity by inference, produces a fluent summary, and hands it to the person who is waiting. The person receives an answer that is confident, complete, and wrong, and receives no signal whatsoever that anything was reconstructed.

The Rendering Casualty withholds meaning. The Reconstruction Casualty replaces it. The second is worse, because the first announces itself.

The core reconstruction test: ask a machine reader to summarise the page and state what it could not determine. If it does not know what it did not know, neither do you. See §4.8.

### 1.9 The Sent-Agent Test

A sent agent is a machine reader acting in response to a present request from a person. The person has asked it to retrieve, read, summarise, compare, navigate, transform, or act upon public information, and is waiting for the result.

The test is simple: would this configuration stop a machine reader that a person sent? If yes, it creates an Admission Casualty and is not ZIC-compliant on public content.

The casualty is the person. The agent is only the vehicle. A refusal may appear in a log as a crawler decision, a WAF rule, a robots response, a JavaScript challenge, or a rate limit. In human terms, information requested by a reader was withheld from that reader.

**Equal conditions are permitted.** ZIC does not require an agent to bypass a login, subscription, payment, consent flow, privacy boundary, or access restriction that applies equally to a human visitor. It prohibits an additional barrier imposed because the visitor is a sent agent.

The test returns a different answer for search indexing and model training. Nobody has sent those crawlers with a present question. Permitting or declining either is a later-use decision. ZIC requires the decision to be explicit, independent, and true; it does not choose the answer for the publisher.

**Reproduction to the sender is retrieval (new in v1.7).** A sent agent may hand the person who sent it the whole page: read aloud, rendered as Markdown, pasted into a chat window, spoken through a car. Vocabularies are now in circulation that classify full reproduction as a use which forfeits an operator’s trusted status, and this specification takes a position before those vocabularies take one for it. Reproduction to the person who asked is not a use of the content. It is the content arriving. A screen reader reproduces every page it reads in full, to one person, on request, and nobody has ever proposed that a screen reader be declared untrusted for doing so. The sent agent that does the same thing is doing the same thing. What the person does with the page afterwards is governed by the content licence (§1.10, object 2), exactly as it would be had she read it with her eyes; what the agent’s operator may retain or redistribute is a later use and is governed by the later-use declarations. Neither question is the delivery question, and the delivery question is the only one §1.9 asks.

### 1.10 Four Things Kept Apart

Four distinct objects are routinely fused on the live web. ZIC keeps them separate.

**1. The licence of this specification.** How another party may use, fork, adapt, or extend ZIC itself. CC BY-SA 4.0: share and adapt with attribution, under the same terms.

**2. The licence of the site's content.** What another party may legally copy, adapt, republish, or otherwise reuse after obtaining it. This is set by the publisher.

**3. The conformance bar.** Whether the site serves sent agents and meets the rendering, delivery, semantic, technical, and validation requirements of this specification. Binary: pass or fail.

**4. The later-use declarations.** Whether search indexing and model training are permitted. Two separate yes-or-no answers, set by the publisher and declared machine-readably.

These answer four different questions — may I fork the rules, may I reuse the content, does this site follow the rules, and may I perform either of these later machine uses — and a document that answers them in one breath answers none of them.

### 1.11 The Single-Sense Rule (new in v1.4)

**No information may be locked behind a single sense.**

That is the whole of the rendering half of this specification. Everything in Part Two and every rendering requirement in Part Three is a consequence of it, and nothing that is not a consequence of it belongs there.

The rule is about information. It is not about decoration, and it has nothing whatsoever to say about beauty.

Colour is not the problem. Colour **as the only carrier of a status, a category, a distinction, or a warning** is the problem, because a person who cannot see the colour cannot receive the information, and neither can the agent she sent. Use whatever colour you like. Say it in words as well.

An image is not the problem. An image **that carries information available nowhere else** is the problem. A decorative image with alt="" transmits nothing and withholds nothing; it is silent by construction and causes no casualty. An informative image without a description is a locked room.

A typeface is not the problem. Emphasis carried **only** by a typeface is the problem, because \<em\> exists and italic does not survive the journey.

Position is not the problem. Meaning carried **only** by position is the problem, which is why DOM order must match reading order.

Size is not the problem. A heading that is **only** large is the problem, because it is a heading to one sense and a paragraph to every other.

The rule generates its own tests. For any element of a page, ask: **is there information here that exists in one sensory channel and nowhere else?** If yes, it must be duplicated into the semantic layer. If no, the element is outside this specification's jurisdiction and the publisher may do as she likes with it.

A ZIC-conformant site may be as visually rich, branded, illustrated, and typographically opinionated as its publisher wishes. It may not keep a single fact where only one sense can reach it.

### 1.12 What ZIC Does Not Govern (new in v1.4)

Standards accumulate scope the way sites accumulate visual encoding, and for the same reason: nobody is watching the boundary. This section watches it.

**ZIC does not govern appearance.** Typography, colour palette, imagery, illustration, iconography, ornament, layout, grid, whitespace, visual identity, and brand are the publisher's business and none of the standard's. A conformant site may look like a Swiss poster, a fanzine, a bank, or a wall of text. ZIC has no opinion and is not entitled to one.

**ZIC does not govern taste.** The reference implementation is austere. That is a preference of its publisher, not a property of the standard, and v1.3 was wrong to write it down as though it were.

**ZIC does not govern search or training policy.** It requires that both be declared, independently and truthfully. It does not require either answer. A publisher who declines both and serves sent agents is fully conformant.

**ZIC does not govern content.** What a site says, whether it is any good, and who it is for are not this specification's concern. Plain language is required only in the sense that meaning must actually be recoverable; a technical document may be as technical as its audience requires.

**ZIC does not govern hosting, framework, or stack.** Parts Five and Six are notes, not requirements. Any stack that delivers the artefacts and passes the checks conforms.

What remains after all of that is the standard: **information reaches the reader, whoever and whatever the reader is.** If a clause in this document cannot be traced to that sentence, the clause is a defect and should be reported.

### 1.13 The Composition of ZIC (amended in v1.5)

ZIC is described as an agent-first standard. That description is a strategy, and it is honest about the strategy, but it is not a complete account of the standard's contents.

The requirements of this specification are the **union** of two sets that overlap heavily and neither of which contains the other.

**What a sent agent requires and a screen reader user does not:** delivery (§1.8), admission (§1.6), a certificate that validates, a robots policy that does not fail closed, an agent surface, machine-readable licence and policy declarations. A screen reader user arrives inside the building. Her browser has already trusted the certificate, already been admitted, already fetched the page. Every one of those requirements is invisible from where she is standing.

**What a human sensory reader requires and an agent does not:** visible focus indicators, keyboard operability, skip links, text scaling to 200% without loss, prefers-reduced-motion, prefers-contrast, and colour contrast ratios. No agent has ever needed a focus ring. In v1.4 this document said these were here because human beings need them, and for no other reason. That was true, and it undersold them: most of this list is derived in §1.15, and the remainder of this section accounts for what is left.

**What both require:** heading hierarchy, landmark structure, descriptive link text, DOM reading order, text alternatives, honest semantics — everything that follows from §1.11.

The overlap is large enough that the strategy works: a site built for agents is very nearly a site built for screen readers, and a publisher motivated entirely by being read by machines will, in the course of pursuing that, remove most of the barriers facing blind people. That is the point, and it needs no apology.

But the sets are not identical, and a specification that pretended otherwise would be lying in a way that its own §1.11 forbids. Neither reader sees all of the terrain. This document is written from both positions at once, and it says so.

Most of the human list no longer needs a separate justification (amended in v1.5). Skip links and focus indicators derive from §1.15. Text scaling and colour contrast were always §1.11 applied to a degraded sense, as §2.1 has said since v1.4. Keyboard operability follows from the founding definition's participation clause: a control that only a pointer can operate has locked an action behind a single input channel. What remains is one requirement this framework cannot honestly derive: **prefers-reduced-motion**. Motion does not withhold information and does not delay it. It can make the reader ill. The requirement is retained — a standard that delivers every fact while inducing vestibular distress in the person reading it has missed the point of being read — but it is retained as what it is: a harm-prevention requirement, the one item in this specification that protects the reader rather than the information. This document forbids dishonest encoding in §1.11 and will not practise it in its own derivations.

One clarification guards the boundary this exception could otherwise breach. If ZIC retains one requirement because it prevents harm, why not every harm — flash thresholds, photosensitive seizure risk, the whole territory of protective design? Because ZIC does not select among harms at all. prefers-reduced-motion is retained because it arrives as a **declaration**: a standard, machine-expressible statement of the reader's own rendering requirements, transmitted in the protocol, of exactly the class this specification already treats as authoritative in §2.1 — prefers-color-scheme, prefers-contrast, the visitor's base font size. The reader has spoken, in the one register a human reader can speak machine-readably, and a specification whose entire subject is honest service to the reader who arrives may not ignore her. Harms that arrive with no declaration — flash limits, seizure risk carried by content itself — require the publisher to police material on behalf of readers who have said nothing. That is real work and it matters, and it belongs to general accessibility and safety standards, WCAG's photosensitivity provisions among them, not to this one (§1.14). The harm is the reader's reason for declaring. The declaration is this specification's reason for obeying.

### 1.14 What ZIC Secures, and What It Does Not (new in v1.4.1; retitled in v1.5)

ZIC guarantees that the meaning of a public page exists in the semantic layer and reaches the reader who asks for it. It does not guarantee that the rendering is optimal for any particular person.

It says nothing about cognitive load, reading level, plain-language alternatives, symbol sets, motor accessibility, timing, seizure risk, or the many other requirements that people with disabilities this specification's author does not have will rightly demand of a page.

This is not an oversight, and it is not modesty. It is the position: **no single rendering is optimal for everyone, and a standard that claimed to produce one would be lying.** The person who needs plain language and the person who needs dense technical precision want opposite pages. The person who needs no motion and the person who needs motion in order to perceive that something has changed want opposite pages. The entire history of Classical Accessibility is the history of pretending that one artefact can serve all of them, and of producing one that serves none of them well.

Generative Accessibility (§1.4) makes the opposite move. It stops attempting the single perfect artefact and instead guarantees a source from which many renderings can be generated. Every such rendering — a simplified-language version, a symbol-set version, a voice rendering, a rendering for a reader nobody has thought of yet — requires that the meaning exist somewhere reachable and honestly structured *before* it can be re-rendered for anyone.

That is what this specification secures. Not a floor beneath a building: the material the building is made of. In v1.4.1 this section's title still said floor while its final paragraphs said substrate. The title has caught up with the argument.

ZIC therefore does not offer a ceiling, and its author does not claim the standing to specify one. It secures the substrate. It leaves the renderings to the people who need them, and to the standards written by those qualified to specify them.

**ZIC is necessary. It is nowhere near sufficient. It is written to be built on.**

### 1.15 Structural Information (new in v1.5)

The structure of a document is information the document carries about itself: where the main content begins, where repeated material ends, what belongs to what, and how the whole is organised. It is information *about* the document rather than *in* it, and this specification has never treated that distinction as a licence to lose it — §3.3 already states that metadata is not decoration. Structural information is subject to §1.11 like any other fact: it may not be locked behind a single sense.

Consider one structural fact: *the main content starts here.* A sighted reader receives it by glance; visual gestalt performs an almost cost-free perceptual skip past the repeated header. An agent receives it by parsing the main element. A screen reader user receives it through landmark navigation. And a sighted keyboard user, navigating sequentially by the Tab key, receives it through — nothing. Browsers do not expose landmark navigation to the Tab key. For that reader, and for that reader alone, the fact exists in no channel at all unless the skip link supplies it.

The skip link is therefore not a human-accessibility requirement standing politely beside the casualty framework. It is the keyboard-modality **rendering** of the same structural fact that the main element renders for the agent and the visual gap renders for the eye. One fact; one rendering per channel that needs it. That is Generative Accessibility in miniature, and it is why the requirement belongs in this specification twice over: once as casualty prevention, and once as evidence that the substrate is real.

Focus indicators have the same shape. *Where am I in this document's interactive sequence* is information. The screen reader announces it. The sighted keyboard user has only the focus ring. Remove the ring and that information is held in no channel whatsoever — which is worse than a single sense, and prohibited by the same rule.

No fifth casualty class is required. The loss of structural information is a Rendering Casualty of the document's own organisation: the meaning was present and the observer could not decode it. The four questions of §1.8 stand unamended, and their elegance is not purchased at the price of an exception.

### 1.16 The Position Principle (new in v1.5, amended in v1.6)

**Equivalent access does not require identical interaction. It requires that every reader can reach the same informational and orientational position through a mechanism appropriate to their channel.**

The sighted reader sees the hierarchy. The screen reader user hears semantic headings and landmarks. The keyboard user is handed a skip link. The agent parses the DOM. These readers do not behave alike, are not addressed alike, and could not be — the equivalence this specification claims was never an equivalence of experience. It is an equivalence of **position**: each reader, by a different road, arrives knowing where the content is, how it is organised, and how to proceed.

The two principles divide the labour cleanly. The Single-Sense Rule (§1.11) governs how information is encoded: no fact may live where only one sense can reach it. The Position Principle governs whether information arrives: no reader may be left short of the position every other reader has reached. A page can pass the first and fail the second — every fact duplicated into the semantic layer, and one class of reader still labouring toward what another receives at a glance. Conformance requires both.

**The principle binds through its derivations (new in v1.6).** The testable content of this principle is exhausted by the requirements derived from it in this document — the skip link, the focus indicator, landmark structure, and their companions in Parts Two and Three. An auditor may not derive a novel failure from this section directly. Labour has no stated threshold, and a principle without a threshold, applied directly as a check, fails whoever the auditor wishes it to fail; taken literally, every screen reader user labours relative to a glance, and the principle would convict every page ever built. Where a reader believes a channel has been left short of position in a way no existing requirement captures, that is a defect report against this specification under §1.12, and the derivation enters through revision. The principle governs the standard. The requirements govern the site.

### 1.17 Normative Language (new in v1.6)

This specification binds with three words, and from this version it defines them. **Must** marks a requirement: conformance fails without it. **Should** marks a recommendation: a practice this specification endorses, whose absence does not affect conformance — and which, where a site adopts it and claims it, is checked as though required. **May** marks a permission.

Earlier versions used the words in these senses without defining them, and in one place — the agent surface, §3.6 — the undefined words were allowed to contradict each other. The correction is in that section. One further rule guards the boundary: where this document says nothing, it means nothing. Silence is not a weak prohibition, and no requirement may be inferred from the absence of a permission. §1.12 states what ZIC does not govern; this section adds that the not-governed cannot be smuggled back in through implication.

### 1.18 The Fourth Purpose (new in v1.7)

As of September 2026 a fourth machine use is being separated from the other three by the operators who perform it and the edge that admits them: the generation of an AI summary in a search result, from content that was permitted to be indexed. The operators designated accountable by the largest edge network must now offer publishers an opt-out from it, and each does so in its own way, through its own controls, with no common machine-readable field.

This specification’s logic already reaches the case. §1.7 says no permission is inferred from another, and a summary is not an index: the index points a future person at the page; the summary stands in for it. Permission to be found is not permission to be replaced. A publisher who holds that view holds it with this specification’s support.

What this specification cannot do is declare the purpose. §1.17 says that where this document says nothing, it means nothing, and the rule guards the standard from itself as much as from its readers. ZIC declares in standard, machine-readable fields, and there is no standard field for summaries. Until there is, the summary decision is a matter between the publisher and each operator, and ZIC neither requires it, records it, nor infers it. A publisher who states her summary policy in llms.txt or in her conformance statement may do so; the statement is hers and not this specification’s. When a standard field exists — in Content Signals, in the IETF’s ai-prefs work, or elsewhere — this section will be revised, and the three declarations of §1.7 will become four. The structure is built to take it. That is the point of keeping the purposes apart.

## Part Two: Design Decisions

This section documents what ZIC requires, what it rules out, and what it leaves alone. Every requirement follows from §1.11. Everything in v1.3 that did not follow from §1.11 has been removed.

### 2.1 What ZIC Requires

**Honest structure.** Headings must be headings, lists must be lists, tables must be tables, and each must be marked up as what it is. Visual appearance may reinforce structure; it may not substitute for it.

**Relative sizing.** Font sizes and spacing should use relative units (rem, em, %) that scale with the visitor's base font size setting. Text must remain readable and complete at 200% without horizontal scrolling or content loss. This is a requirement about *scaling*, not about *size*: set whatever base size you like.

**High contrast defaults.** Default text colours must meet WCAG AA contrast ratios against their background: 4.5:1 for normal text, 3:1 for large text. The prefers-contrast: more media query must be implemented and must raise the rendering to AAA ratios — 7:1 and 4.5:1. The prefers-color-scheme media query must be respected; the visitor's OS-level settings are authoritative.

Contrast is the one visual property this specification does govern, and the reason is that it is not decoration. Contrast is whether a degraded sense can receive the text at all — which places it squarely inside §1.11. A publisher may choose any colours she likes. She may not choose colours that lock the text away from the people who need contrast to read it.

**Two things are true about this requirement, and v1.6 keeps them apart (amended in v1.6).** That contrast must be governed is derived: it is §1.11 applied to a degraded sense, and no version of this document has needed to apologise for it. What ratio suffices is not derived and cannot be. No principled framework generates thresholds; thresholds come from measurement, and these come from the empirical vision research underlying WCAG. Earlier versions required AAA as though 7:1 followed from the casualty concept, and by §1.12’s own test that was a defect: a number the framework did not produce, wearing the uniform of a derivation. The default is therefore the measured baseline, AA. The readers beyond the baseline are served by the mechanism this specification already treats as authoritative (§1.13): the reader’s own declaration. A reader who needs more contrast says so, machine-readably, through prefers-contrast: more, and a conformant site answers with AAA. The law is derived; the constants are measured; and the document now says which is which.

**Structural metadata.** Page titles, meta descriptions, Open Graph tags, Schema.org JSON-LD, sitemaps, robots.txt, and llms.txt are not optional decoration. They are the site's interface with agents, indexers, and assistive technologies. They must be accurate, complete, and meaningful.

**Skip links.** A skip-to-main-content link as the first focusable element is required on every page. Derivation at §1.15.

**Focus indicators.** Visible, clear focus indicators are required on every user-operable control. The browser default is acceptable; removing or weakening it is not. Derivation at §1.15.

**Suppressed outlines on landmark targets.** A landmark that is focusable only programmatically — typically \<main tabindex="-1"\> as the destination of a skip link — may suppress its focus outline. It is a destination, not a control. This exception is narrow and applies only to elements with tabindex="-1" that no keyboard sequence can reach.

**Reading order.** Visual reading order must match DOM order.

### 2.2 What ZIC Rules Out

Each prohibition below is a direct consequence of §1.11. There are no others.

**Information carried by colour alone.** Status, category, hierarchy, warning, or any other meaningful distinction must be encoded in text or structure. Colour may reinforce it. Colour may not be the only place it lives.
